documents.title: Field guide to retrieval evaluation
documents.body: A study guide for building a small, defensible search evaluation. Start with a ranking rubric and track why each retrieval method fails.
documents.subtitle: A practical guide to query sets, rankings and evidence
sections: Design the query set

Collect questions that match how people look for things. Include exact identifiers, paraphrases and ambiguous requests. Keep variants in the same split so a tuning query cannot reveal the answer to an evaluation query.
Judge the evidence

Mark a result as useful when it contains the information needed to answer the query. Record the relevant page or sentence. Multiple captures may answer a query, and near copies should be judged consistently.
Choose metrics by task

Use Recall@5 to ask whether a useful result was in the first five. Reciprocal rank tracks the first relevant result. nDCG rewards high placement for the most useful results when judgments have grades.
Inspect failed queries

Run a lexical baseline before adding embeddings. Track misses caused by document parsing, reference tokenization and ranking errors separately. Report the final query set composition alongside the scores.
appendix: A relevance grade of 2 means the result answers the query directly. A grade of 1 means it gives context but needs another source. A grade of 0 means it is unrelated or wrong. Score the evidence before seeing the rank order.

When only positions 2 and 4 are relevant, Recall@5 is 1.0 and reciprocal rank is 0.5. If the position 2 document is the more useful of the two, nDCG rewards it more than the position 4 document. These examples use invented judgments.

documents.title: Sentence embeddings in practice
documents.body: A primer on finding relevant passages when searchers and authors use different vocabulary.
documents.subtitle: From text passages to local semantic search
sections: What a vector represents
A sentence encoder maps short text into a sequence of numbers. For retrieval, queries and passages use the same encoder. Normalizing vectors lets a dot product rank their cosine similarity.
Keep retrieval tied to a passage

Split long notes into overlapping chunks and save page or line numbers with each vector. When a result opens, give the reader the text that matched. Whole-document vectors can hide a useful phrase inside a long file.
Separate index versions
Store the model revision and chunking strategy with the vectors. Re-index records when either changes. A stale vector can point to text that a person has already edited.
Where meaning is insufficient
Embeddings often handle paraphrases, but exact order codes and abbreviated names can be harder. Keep a keyword route so the exact spelling remains useful. Show an excerpt with related captures.

documents.title: Avoiding leakage in model evaluation
documents.body: A worksheet for separating development examples from final evaluation before comparing models.
documents.subtitle: An experiment worksheet for student projects
sections: Split by the real unit

If several notes describe the same event, keep them in one group. Splitting individual notes can leak names, near duplicates and labels into both sets. Put entire groups in training, development or final evaluation.
Fit transforms after splitting
Learn vocabulary, centering or feature scales using only training data. Apply those frozen transforms to development and final inputs. A pipeline makes this boundary easier to maintain.
Tune once, evaluate once
Use development examples to choose thresholds and features. Decide what metric matters before opening the final set. If final results guide more changes, reserve a fresh evaluation set.
Write the sampling note
Record sample sizes, label rules and disagreements. A synthetic dataset can test a particular workflow. Its metrics do not establish performance for an uncurated population.

documents.title: An INT8 quantization lab
documents.body: An original lab worksheet for comparing size, latency and quality between float and integer models.
documents.subtitle: Measure the trade-offs on one CPU
sections: Establish the comparison
Choose one float checkpoint and one quantized export of the same model. Record the revision, runtime, thread count, prompt lengths and batching. Run both on the same device.
Inspect storage and latency
Measure bytes downloaded and distinguish model files from runtime files. Report a cold load and a warmed query separately. Capture repeated timings and show the median with a slower percentile.
Compare quality on fixed cases
Run both models over identical examples. For embeddings, compare top results rather than only vector error. Near-identical vectors can still move a crucial distractor above the target.
Read the result in context
Smaller weights can reduce transfer and memory costs. Faster inference depends on operators, hardware and runtime support. Record cases where a kernel falls back to an unexpected path.

documents.title: An OCR quality worksheet
documents.body: A practical worksheet for measuring OCR quality on screenshots, receipts and multi-column pages.
documents.subtitle: Evaluate transcription and evidence separately
sections: Make ground truth specific
Transcribe the intended reading order and mark ambiguous characters. Keep the reference separate from recognized output. Decide whether case and whitespace matter before scoring.
Check characters and words
Character error rate divides edit distance by the reference character count. Word error rate applies the same idea to word tokens. One wrong digit may matter more than a missing space.
Group the failure cases
Compare clean text, faint thermal print, skew and columns separately. Check whether recognition or reading order is responsible. A well-rendered page can still yield lines in the wrong order.
Evaluate entity extraction too
Check the amount, date and reference code against the image. Store OCR text and supporting evidence so corrections can be reviewed. Flag uncertain dates before creating reminders.
appendix: Reference: Gate B14 at 18:20. OCR: Gate B14 at 18:ZO. Count both character substitutions and mark the departure time as a failed extracted field.
Keep the original image, record the OCR configuration and log corrections. Review an amount or date before accepting a suggested action. Add difficult examples to a new validation set.

notes.title: When vocabulary does not match
notes.body: Sentence embeddings retrieve relevant passages even when a note and the question use different words. Try asking about reducing a model's storage size to find the INT8 worksheet. Keep exact reference matching available for identifiers.

notes.title: Offline experiment metric checklist
notes.body: Use Recall@5 for finding what matters, MRR for the first relevant result, and nDCG for graded judgments. Track response latency separately from relevance. Record model revision, hardware, and the evaluation split.

notes.title: Working note on rank fusion
notes.body: Reciprocal rank fusion combines positions rather than raw scores. A single complete reference is usually stronger evidence than scattered vocabulary matches. Preserve the match explanation and compare rankings by query type.

notes.title: Reading a SQLite query plan
notes.body: Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for slow SELECT queries. A SEARCH line can indicate an index lookup. A SCAN can still suit small tables. Check index column order against WHERE and ORDER BY before measuring again.

notes.title: IndexedDB durability checklist
notes.body: Group changes to records and indexes in a transaction. Avoid await between dependent IndexedDB requests if it lets the transaction close. After a migration, verify that old attachment Blobs still open. Keep a portable backup path.

notes.title: Testing focus and contrast
notes.body: Use visible keyboard focus and check that it returns to the opener when a dialog closes. Review text contrast in both themes and repeat at a narrow viewport. Token contrast measurements cannot replace testing actual rendered states.

notes.title: The shape of a useful note
notes.body: A good note is a small container for a good thought. Keep the source, write down what made it interesting, and give it a title you can find later.

notes.title: A note on paying attention
notes.body: The things we notice are the things we get to keep.
